Uncertainty abounds. In the U.S., AI has catalyzed a historic wave of investment. Companies have announced plans for more than $2 trillion in specific data center construction projects. So far, only a fraction of this has been realized.3 This investment is already showing up in output data. And there is evidence of spillovers to other parts of the economy—in the price of chips and high-tech equipment, construction wages, and electricity costs. What I want to stress today is that this is not simply a North American phenomenon.

As AI adoption spreads, younger workers may continue to be disproportionately affected, and firms may need to take innovative and creative steps to train their future workforce. I am watching carefully the speed and acceleration of AI adoption across sectors and noting evidence of the changing mix of jobs within firms. [OFFICIAL] types of tasks and jobs are already being created, and I remain hopeful that job creation will be able to keep pace with job destruction. I will now turn to my outlook on the U.S. economy. U.S. [OFFICIAL] Outlook Overall economic growth in the U.S. is strong—and accelerating. The labor market remains solid, and, of great concern to me, inflation is well above the Fed's 2 percent target and has been for 67 months.

I will start my forecast, as I typically do, with the price-stability side of our dual mandate, because, given the current state of the economy, this is my focus. Then, I will give my views on the path of monetary policy. One theme I want to emphasize is that waiting to act when a policy adjustment is required has a cost. Inflation Inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, has exceeded the 2 percent target described in our framework for nearly six years. Based on U.S. inflation data released last week, it is estimated that the 12-month change in the PCE price index was 3.8 percent in October. The 12-month change in core prices—which exclude volatile food and energy costs—was 3.2 percent in October.

The core measure underscores that, while energy is a significant contributor to inflation, the sources of price pressure facing American families are increasingly varied. Inflation soared in 2021 and 2022 because of supply disruptions and surging demand following the reopening of the U.S. and economies around the world as the global pandemic abated. The Fed, much like other central banks, responded by aggressively raising interest rates to fight inflation. I supported those actions as soon as I joined the Fed. From the middle of 2022 until the early part of last year, inflation moved down and appeared to be on a sustainable path back toward the 2 percent objective. However, a series of economic shocks over the past 18 months—including significant changes to trade policy, geopolitical developments, and massive investment in technological infrastructure—partially reversed that progress.

Annual inflation in the U.S. has been steadily above 3 percent for much of this year, and, thus far, there is little evidence inflation is declining. In fact, the most recent inflation release showed that prices are rising briskly in a very broad range of categories—including airfare, appliances, furniture, hotels, and restaurants, to name a few. Labor market and output Next, I will turn to the labor market, the other half of the dual mandate assigned to the Fed by Congress. The U.S. labor market is solid, with still-low unemployment and consistent, though modest, hiring. The unemployment rate was 4.1 percent in October and has trended down modestly for nearly a year. As I have already mentioned, there is little evidence that AI is producing a significant imprint on the aggregate unemployment rate.

Other data indicate the labor market is roughly in balance and gradually improving. Payrolls climbed by 165,000 in October, and some evidence is emerging that hiring is broadening to a wider array of sectors. Job openings in September were largely unchanged at 7.5 million, and initial unemployment claims, a proxy for layoffs, remain near historical lows—at a four-week moving average of about 195,000. Despite signs of strength, some Americans remain understandably frustrated with the state of the labor market. The "low hire" environment is particularly challenging for new entrants. And wages are growing but not enough to overcome the damaging effects of inflation. Still, low unemployment is consistent with achieving our maximum-employment mandate, and, therefore, as a monetary policymaker, I am more focused on the inflation side of our remit.

[OFFICIAL] output in the U.S. has accelerated. GDP rose at a 3.4 percent annual pace in the third quarter, a pickup from already solid growth in the first half. The AI infrastructure buildout I previously discussed is a significant contributor to this acceleration. At the same time, American consumers have proven to be resilient, with real household spending rising an annualized 3.8 percent last quarter despite higher energy prices and broader inflationary pressure. Monetary Policy This leads to the path of U.S. monetary policy. The Federal Open Market Committee in September raised the target range for the federal funds rate to 3-3/4 to 4 percent to support a timelier return to the 2 percent objective. I supported that decision. At the most recent meeting, in October, the Committee voted to hold the policy rate steady.

I dissented from that decision. I preferred to raise the target range another 1/4 percentage point. Two main reasons informed my decision to dissent. First, in my view, financial conditions are too accommodative at a time when inflation remains stubbornly above target, with no clear signs of disinflation in train. The current stance of policy does not appear to be curtailing the AI buildout, and equity prices continue to support consumer spending. As a result, holding our policy rate steady will lead to a positive and widening output gap and increasing inflationary pressure. Indeed, we are seeing elevated inflation in a broad swath of goods and services. I see the act of holding the rate steady as much a monetary policy action as the act of increasing the rate.

Second, my vote reflected the urgency I feel to tackle inflation. Inflation has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward. Furthermore, waiting longer to implement rate increases risks getting behind the curve. If we fall behind, additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up, which could increase stress on our financial system and have unnecessarily damaging effects on American households. I have previously discussed my growing concern about the direction of inflation in several speeches this year.8 I have called inflation unacceptably high. This remains my view. I have articulated my frustration that inflation has moved in the wrong direction as a series of shocks stacked upon each other.

In addition, I noted that the extended time inflation had exceeded our target was an important part of my calculation. In a different environment, the Committee could afford to be patient, but I continue to believe that in this economic climate we do not have that luxury. I am skeptical that September's single 1/4 point rate increase will be enough to change the path of inflation. The number and magnitude of future adjustments should be informed by observations of the economy's reaction to our policy actions. The inflation data received since the September rate increase, including reports last week, fail to provide me with sufficient evidence that inflation is returning to a sustainable path. Conclusion Allow me to close where I began.

The forces I have described today—geopolitical conflict, shifting trade relationships, and the buildout of AI—extend beyond national borders and weigh on the minds of monetary policymakers, including those in the U.S. and here in Chile. In terms of my view of U.S. policy, there is an overriding issue we must confront: Inflation has been above our target for far too long. I take great encouragement from the resilience of the labor market and the American economy—and the promise of the technologies now reshaping it. This promise will be best supported if we restore stable prices on which sustainable growth depends. Delivering on both sides of the dual mandate is the task before the Federal Reserve, and I am committed to seeing it through.
